analysis.one_liner: Bars DHS from building or expanding warehouse, tent, and other large-scale immigration detention centers.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2026 and referred to two House committees, the bill has received no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement from creating or expanding warehouse, tent, modular, and other large-scale immigration detention facilities, whether run by the government or by contractors. It would block existing federal funds from being spent, reprogrammed, or transferred for these facilities, and it would move money already obligated for them into affordable health care and housing. The bill's findings cite a planned $38.3 billion acquisition and retrofit program, deaths in detention, and poor conditions as the reasons for the ban.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants at risk of detention and their families and communities, especially people who would otherwise be held in converted warehouses and tent facilities; communities near proposed sites, which the bill says would face strained water, power, and local resources; and people who would gain from the redirected funds going to affordable health care and housing.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits DHS and ICE from establishing, expanding, converting, or renovating warehouses, industrial facilities, tents, soft-sided structures, and modular units for housing, processing, or detaining people under civil immigration authority, whether operated directly or by a contractor. [S2] [S1]

Blocks any already-appropriated federal money from being obligated, expended, reprogrammed, or transferred to build or operate new detention models, closing off the announced plan to spend roughly $38.3 billion acquiring and retrofitting warehouses into large-scale detention centers. [S2]
Directs money already obligated for new detention models to be transferred to needed services such as affordable health care and housing. [S2]

The bill's findings cite 33 reported deaths in immigration detention in 2025 and 13 so far in 2026, along with documented medical neglect, overcrowding, and harsh conditions, as the basis for the ban. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: DHS and ICE lose the ability to build, lease, or contract for new large-scale detention capacity, and the private companies and construction firms that would win the roughly $38.3 billion in warehouse acquisition and retrofit work lose that business. The bill does not close existing detention facilities or end current contracts, so current operations continue.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves every existing detention facility and current contract untouched; it stops new and expanded facilities but does not shrink the detention system that the bill itself describes as having serious conditions problems. [S2]

Under current enforcement operations, halting new capacity could strain the existing detention system, and the bill offers no alternative plan for where people in immigration proceedings would be held while it redirects obligated funds to health care and housing. [S2]
The prohibition and funding transfer take effect immediately on enactment, with no transition period for facilities already in development. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would stop a very large, rapid expansion of immigration detention into buildings not designed for it, which its own findings link to deaths and unsafe conditions, and it moves the same money to health care and housing. The honest cost is that it provides no replacement capacity for the current detention system while leaving that system's existing problems untouched, and it gives no transition for projects already underway.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Judiciary and Homeland Security committees in April 2026 and to a Judiciary subcommittee the next day, and it has sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced H.R. 8494 on April 23, 2026, with 13 original cosponsors. [S1] [S4]
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Homeland Security Committee on the day of introduction. [S4]
On April 24, 2026, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Oversight, Investigations, and Accountability; no further action appears in the record. [S4]

The bill would prohibit DHS and ICE from establishing or expanding warehouse, tent, modular, and similar detention facilities and would bar existing funds from being spent or transferred for them, redirecting obligated amounts to health care and housing. [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because no restriction has been enacted, DHS keeps its authority to acquire and retrofit warehouses and other facilities for detention, and the private contractors and construction firms in line for that work keep the expansion pipeline open. The roughly $38.3 billion in planned detention spending remains available.

industries.industry: Private prison and detention facility operators
industries.note: The bill bars DHS from entering, renewing, or extending contracts for new detention models, including warehouse and tent facilities operated by contractors, cutting these companies out of a planned $38.3 billion expansion. Their existing detention contracts would continue, but the bill's revenue model depends on detaining immigrants, which runs directly against the people the bill protects.

industries.industry: Construction and industrial facility retrofit contractors
industries.note: The bill blocks the announced program to spend about $38.3 billion acquiring and retrofitting warehouses and industrial buildings into detention centers, eliminating that construction pipeline. Those profits would come from building facilities the bill's findings describe as unsuited to human detention.

The bill transfers money obligated for new detention models to affordable health care and housing services, directing federal spending away from detention and toward those providers and the people they serve.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in two committees with support only from Democrats in a Republican-led House, and no hearing or markup has been scheduled. Absent a change in House control or attachment to an appropriations bill, it is likely to die without a vote when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
